sections.body:
Attachment is the part of a person that notices whether an important other person is available, and what the person does about it. In an adult romantic relationship it is the set of promises a person brings to a partner, the rules they use to read that partner's behaviour, and the speed at which they settle down when the partner is not there. It is a background system: most of the time it is quiet, and a reader sees it only when something changes. A reply does not arrive, a voice changes, a door closes. The system notices the change, makes a plan, and acts, and what the person feels afterwards is often the first sign that the system was running at all.

Behind the system sits a **working model**: the set of assumptions a person carries about how other people answer when they reach out. A working model says roughly what a reply means, how long a silence can last, how much closeness a person can carry, and what happens if they ask for more. Most people hold these rules without words: they are felt as a sense of what is normal, and applied without being noticed. A working model is built from earlier relationships and kept up to date by later ones: family first, then friends, then the first relationships that mattered. How much of an adult pattern comes from the earliest years is still argued over. One account puts most of the weight on early relationships, because the first pattern is the one that forms fastest. Another puts the weight on what a person has learned since, and on the relationship they are in now. A third says that the situation itself does much of the work in the moment: a long-distance relationship, a new city, a heavy month at work. No account has settled the question, and this article does not need them to. Whatever the weight, the person still brings a model, and the model still predicts what they will do next.

The **secure base** is the person or the relationship that lets a person move away and still stay steady. It is the place the person can leave from: a new job in another city, a week with friends, a difficult conversation with somebody else. A person with a secure base can be apart and not panic, because the bond is treated as still there. A secure base is a function rather than a feeling you can measure, and it does not require a perfect partner. It requires a partner who can be found again: who answers, who comes back, and whose answer is believable. Two people can have a bond that is warm on paper and still have no secure base, because the bond is never tested by distance.

This article is about adult romantic relationships, and it describes patterns rather than people. Two people can live with the same pattern and handle it very differently. The same person can show different patterns with different partners, and a person can change over the years. What the article gives the reader is a vocabulary for the pattern and a short routine for working with it, and nothing that decides whether a relationship is good.
examples: Attachment is the system that notices whether the other person is available.
In an adult relationship, the working model is about this partner now, not about childhood.
A secure base lets a person be away and still feel steady.
The bond has never been tested by distance, so nobody knows yet whether it holds.
sections.heading: What attachment is

terms.example: Her attachment is the system that tells her a partner is not there, before she has any words for it.
terms.gloss: The part of a person that notices whether an important other person is available, and what the person does about it.

terms.example: My working model says that people get busy and come back, so I wait.
terms.gloss: The set of assumptions a person carries about how other people answer when they reach out.

terms.example: His sister was his secure base long before he had a partner of his own.
terms.gloss: The person or relationship a person can move away from and still feel steady in.

sections.body:
The model has three parts, and they run in order. First, the assumed availability: what the person takes for granted about how available the partner will be, how quickly a reply comes, what a quiet evening means, whether a partner who is busy has gone or is simply occupied. Second, the signal: the event that shows more distance than the model assumed. Third, the recovery: the thing that brings the person back down. Most trouble in a relationship happens in the gap between the first part and the second, because the model is a set of rules about what is normal and those rules are usually older than the current partner.

The event that shows more distance than the model assumed is the **trigger**. A trigger is not a fact about the partner's mind; it is a fact about the gap between what the person assumed and what arrived. A partner who is two hours late, busy for a day, or silent after a difficult conversation is a trigger if the model assumed constant contact. The same event is nothing to another person. One reader sees a missed call and reads it as a sign that something is wrong; another sees a missed call and reads it as a Tuesday. The event is shared. The reading is not, and the reading decides what happens next.

The recovery is the part most often overlooked, because the partner usually watches the alarm rather than the recovery. A clear answer settles one person; presence settles another; a routine, a walk, a glass of water settles a third. The model also predicts which recovery will work, because the model decides what counts as evidence that the bond is still there. Asking the same person for a different kind of reassurance, again and again, usually fails: the answer was never the thing that was missing. Because the model is a set of rules and not only a feeling, it can be examined. Any strong reaction can be put into three questions: what did I assume, what did I see, and what would settle me? Naming the three is the first practical use of the model, because it turns a feeling into something a partner can be told about.
examples: The trigger is the gap between what I assumed and what arrived.
A busy evening is a trigger for one reader and nothing at all for another.
What settles me is a clear answer, not more time.
sections.heading: The working model in three parts

terms.example: One missed call was the trigger, and the rest of the evening went into reading the silence.
terms.gloss: The event that makes a person read a partner as less available than the person assumed.

sections.body:
The vocabulary of adult attachment has four words in common use, and each one describes how a person reads availability: **secure**, **anxious**, **avoidant** and **fearful-avoidant**. They are not scores, and they do not say how good a relationship is or how decent a person is. A person is **secure** when the model assumes the partner is available and the bond does not have to be tested every hour. Secure people can be disappointed without falling apart, they can ask for what they need, and they can hear a difficult answer without treating it as a verdict on the relationship.

A person is **anxious** when the model assumes that availability can be withdrawn at any moment, and the person reads every change in the partner's attention as a sign that the bond is at risk. Anxious does not mean dramatic, and it does not mean clingy; it describes the strength of the alarm and the way availability is read. When the partner pulls away, the anxious person reaches: messages, calls, questions, and often a test that the partner is supposed to pass. The partner feels the pressure without being able to see the machinery behind it.

A person is **avoidant** when the model treats closeness as a cost: more closeness means less independence, more demands, less room. The person does not want to be handled, and often pulls back exactly when the other person asks for more. Avoidant does not mean uncaring. It usually means that the bond is real and the sense of self inside the bond feels fragile, so the system reduces contact before the bond can damage it.

A person is **fearful-avoidant** when the model wants closeness and fears it at the same time: the person reaches and withdraws, asks for more and then wants less. Some accounts treat this as a third style with its own machinery. Others treat it as a mix of the two patterns above, held together by a strong fear of loss, and describe the person as moving along both lines rather than sitting in a third box. That argument is open, and so is a second one: whether these four words are best read as separate types or as points on two lines, one for how far a person reaches and one for how much a person protects. The words are useful either way, because they describe what a person did in a moment rather than what the person is.
examples: Secure means the person can be disappointed and stay in the conversation.
Anxious describes how availability is read, not how loud the person is.
Avoidant is a way of protecting independence, not a measure of caring.
Fearful-avoidant reaches and withdraws in the same afternoon.
sections.heading: The four words for the pattern

terms.example: She is secure with him, so she says she is upset instead of guessing.
terms.gloss: Describing a person who takes the partner's availability for granted and stays steady when it wobbles.

terms.example: When he was busy, his anxious side read the quiet as a message about him.
terms.gloss: Describing a person who reads any drop in a partner's availability as a sign that the bond is at risk.

terms.example: His avoidant side called for less contact at the moment he needed it most.
terms.gloss: Describing a person who leans away when closeness increases, to protect independence.

terms.example: Fearful-avoidant behaviour often looks like pulling back right after reaching out.
terms.gloss: Describing a person who wants closeness and is afraid of it at the same time.

sections.body:
The secure person looks for a partner who stays in the room when the conversation turns hard. The fear is not abandonment; it is being taken for granted, and a bond that thins into routine without anybody noticing. When the partner pulls away, the secure person does the smallest sensible thing: asks what is wrong, waits for the answer, and does not fill the silence with a story about the partner's motives. What settles the system is a plain answer and the same closeness that was there before the question. The other three styles run the same machinery in a different direction, and two words name the two directions: **hyperactivation** and **deactivation**.

Hyperactivation is the rising of the alarm. Attention narrows onto the partner, the sign of distance is read as bigger than it is, and the urge to act becomes fast and hard to pause. It is what turns three unanswered messages into an hour of checking the phone, and what makes a person ask the same question in three different ways. The anxious style runs on this. The person looks for proof that the partner is still there: a reply, a plan, a mention in the next day's conversation. The fear is that the partner's interest is fading and the relationship is ending. When the partner pulls away, the system runs **reassurance-seeking**, asking for the answer again and again, because a clear answer settles it only for a few minutes. What actually settles it is predictable contact: a message that arrives when it was promised, and a partner who says what is happening instead of leaving a gap to be filled.

Deactivation is the lowering of the alarm. When closeness increases, the system turns attention away from the bond and towards the task in front of it: work, the car, the screen, the children, the clean kitchen. The alarm stops, and with it the sense of what is at stake. The avoidant style runs on this. The person looks for a partner who allows closeness without requiring it at every moment. The fear is losing control of their own life, or being hurt so badly that it is better to step back first. When the partner pulls away, almost nothing happens, and that silence is the hardest thing in the relationship to read. What settles the system is space with a stated end: an hour, a walk, a return time, and no demand for an explanation of the space itself.

Between the two directions sits a common move. When a person feels the bond slipping, they try to get it back, and the attempt is **protest behaviour**. It can look like pursuit, with more messages, more questions and more attention, or like **withdrawal**, which is the same move pointed the other way: less contact, less talk, a closed door. The two styles differ in which way they point, and a couple can end up in a loop where one person's pursuit produces the other's withdrawal. The fearful-avoidant person runs both. They want closeness and safety together, which is the hardest combination to ask for, and they fear rejection and abandonment in the same breath. When the partner pulls away, they reach and withdraw, and the alarm turns up and down in the same hour. What settles this pattern is predictability, small and consistent contact, and permission to slow down without being pushed.
examples: Hyperactivation makes the sign of distance bigger than it is.
Deactivation is not indifference; it is the alarm being turned down.
Protest behaviour tries to get the bond back, not to win an argument.
Withdrawal usually makes the other person reach harder.
sections.heading: What each style looks for, fears and does

terms.example: Hyperactivation turned three unanswered messages into an hour of checking the phone.
terms.gloss: The rising of the alarm when a partner seems unavailable, which sharpens attention and speeds the urge to act.

terms.example: Deactivation looked like a tidy desk and a long shift at the office.
terms.gloss: The lowering of the alarm when closeness increases, which turns attention away from the bond and towards the task in front of it.

terms.example: Reassurance-seeking is asking the same question until the answer changes.
terms.gloss: Asking a partner repeatedly to confirm that the relationship is still there.

terms.example: Her protest behaviour was sending the message twice and then three times.
terms.gloss: The behaviour a person uses to get a partner's attention back when they feel the bond is slipping.

terms.example: Withdrawal is answering with less, not more, when the other person asks for more.
terms.gloss: Pulling back from a partner and reducing contact when closeness or conflict increases.

sections.body:
A pattern is easier to work with when it is written as signals rather than as a label. The table sets the four styles against four things: what the style looks for, what it fears, how it complains, and what it needs to hear. The first three columns describe the pattern. The fourth column is the only one a partner can act on, and it is the column worth reading twice.

Read the rows as tendencies rather than instructions. A person moves along these lines day to day, and two people in the same row can behave very differently. The table says what usually happens, not what always happens.

The third column is where two partners usually meet each other wrongly. One person's complaint raises the other person's alarm, and the raised alarm produces a complaint of the opposite kind: more messages produce less talk, and less talk produces more messages. Naming the move in advance, saying out loud what I do when I get scared, breaks that loop, because the other person can then read the behaviour as a signal instead of as a verdict.

The fourth column is the part to carry into a conversation. Every cell says what the person needs to hear, and every cell is something a partner can say, repeat and act on. A person who has read this table is not diagnosing anybody. They are learning what to listen for and what to offer.
examples: The table names four columns: what the style looks for, what it fears, how it complains and what it needs to hear.
The two partners usually meet each other wrongly in the third column.
The fourth column is the only one a partner can act on.
sections.heading: The styles against the signals

rows: Secure: the bond is taken as still there.
A partner who can say what is wrong and stay in the conversation.
Being taken for granted, and a bond that thins into routine.
Directly and once: I felt left out yesterday, and I want to hear the rest of it.
That the question was worth asking, and that the answer is about the moment, not about the bond.
Anxious: availability may be withdrawn at any moment.
Proof that the partner is still there: a reply, a plan, a mention.
That the partner's interest is fading and the relationship is ending.
Repeatedly, through messages and questions that test the answer.
A clear answer, a specific time, and contact that arrives when it was promised.
Avoidant: closeness can cost independence.
A partner who allows closeness without requiring it at every moment.
Losing control of their own life, or being hurt before they can move.
By going quiet, changing the subject, or leaving the room.
That the space is welcome, and the exact time the person will be back.
Fearful-avoidant: closeness and safety are wanted together.
Closeness and safety at once, which is the hardest combination to ask for.
Rejection and abandonment at the same time.
In both directions at once: reaching out and then pulling back.
That the person can slow down, and that the door stays open.

sections.body:
The routine is short, it needs no equipment, and it works with any of the four styles. It is not a treatment, and it does not repair a relationship that is broken for other reasons. It is maintenance for the moment after a partner pulls away, because that is the moment where the pattern does most of its damage.

The order is the point. The first step puts the trigger in words, so the reaction stops running in the background. The second replaces a test with a question a partner can answer. The third asks the person to offer what they can actually give, instead of what they wish the partner would do. The fourth translates the style into a clear signal, so the other person is not left to guess. The fifth repairs quickly, because the longer the gap, the bigger the story that grows in it.

None of the steps asks the reader to become a different person. They ask the reader to make one move that the pattern would not make on its own: to say the quiet part first, to ask rather than test, to give what is real, and to come back before the distance hardens.
examples: The trigger was the missed call, not the argument that came after it.
I asked a question with room for an answer, instead of a test.
I can give you twenty minutes now and a decision tomorrow morning.
I went back to the moment, not to the accusation.
sections.heading: Five steps for working with your own style
steps: Name the trigger. Write down the last moment when you read your partner as less available: the missed call, the flat answer, the evening without a message. Name the event first, then the sentence you added to it. The event is a fact; the sentence is a model, and a model can be checked.

Ask instead of testing. Say what you saw and what you want, and give the partner a question that can be answered: 'You were quiet last night — are you annoyed with me, or busy?' A test is a question with the answer written into it; a real question has room for an answer you did not expect.

Offer the thing you can actually give. Say what you can do tonight, such as twenty minutes now and a decision tomorrow morning, instead of what you wish the other person would do. An offer can be accepted and refused; a wish can only be disappointed.

Give the partner the signal your style hides. If you withdraw, say when you will be back. If you seek reassurance, say how much you need to hear it and how often. If you read distance, say what would settle you and how fast. The other person cannot meet a need they cannot hear.

Repair fast after a rupture. Go back to the moment rather than the accusation: 'This morning I heard the word fine, and I decided it meant the end of us.' The shorter the gap, the smaller the repair, and the less the other person has to work out alone.

sections.body:
A style is a way of protecting, not a verdict. Each pattern protects something. The secure person protects the ordinary pace of a life. The anxious person protects against being left without warning. The avoidant person protects independence. The fearful-avoidant person protects against being left, in both directions at once. Nobody installs this system on purpose, and it works well enough most of the time to stay.

A partner is not a diagnosis. Saying that your partner is anxious describes a pattern inside a relationship, not a label on a person. The same person may be calm with somebody else and anxious with you, and that says something about the relationship and the history, not about their worth. This vocabulary is a working tool for adults, not a clinical instrument. If one of you is doing badly in a way that these words do not explain, a professional is a better instrument than a label.

People can change, and the term for it is **earned security**: the capacity to feel safe in a relationship, learned later rather than carried in from earlier life. People learn it in a relationship that stays, in therapy, and in the slow practice of asking instead of testing. How much change is possible, and what makes it happen, is still argued over. One account treats the early pattern as largely fixed, so that later experience can only soften it. Another treats the model as a working model in the true sense, something that keeps being updated by what the person goes through. The debate is open, and the practical answer does not wait for it: a person can change, and the steps in this article are the small part of how.

And nothing here decides whether a relationship is good. Two people can share a style and be in a good relationship. Two people with different styles can be in a bad one. The pattern describes the machinery; the relationship is what the two people build with it.
examples: A style is a way of protecting, not a verdict.
My partner is anxious in this relationship; that is not a label on a person.
People can change, and the change can be learned later in life.
Nothing in the pattern decides whether the relationship is good.
sections.heading: What a style is, and what it is not

terms.example: Her earned security came from a relationship that stayed, after years of ones that did not.
terms.gloss: The capacity to feel safe in a relationship, learned later in life rather than carried in from earlier life.

sections.body:
These are the sentences that are hardest to find in the moment and easiest to use once they are written down. They come in four groups: asking for reassurance, asking for space, answering a partner who has gone quiet, and saying that you are not going anywhere.

The first two groups are requests. They name a need and a shape: how much, how long, and by when. The third group is an answer, and it is for the moment when the other person has already gone quiet. The fourth group is for the moment when the bond needs to be held still, and the plainest sentence is usually the strongest one.
examples: I need to hear that we are alright. Can you say it once, plainly?
I know you are busy. I am asking because my head has already decided that something is wrong.
Can you answer me once now, and then we can leave it?
I need an hour to myself tonight. I am back at nine, and I am not disappearing.
I am not angry with you. I am overloaded, and I will explain it after I have eaten.
Give me an hour and a time to come back, and I will take the hour properly.
I noticed you went quiet after my message. Do you want to talk about it now or later?
I sent three messages because I was anxious, not because you had done anything wrong.
If you need space, say so, and tell me when you will be back.
I am not going anywhere tonight. Sit down and tell me about it.
I am still here in the morning. We can finish this tomorrow.
You are not too much for me to want. Ask me again tomorrow if you need to.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

item.summary: Attachment styles describe the promises a person brings to a partner, the way they read availability, and what they do when a partner is unavailable. After reading this you can name the four styles, describe what each one looks for and fears, recognise the signals that switch your own pattern on, and say what you need in words your partner can act on.
item.title: Attachment Styles in Romantic Relationships
